video_title: What Investors Get Wrong About Trend Following | Philippe Jordan | Top Traders Unplugged | Ep. 154
gist: CFM International president Philippe Jordan argues trend following is a ~0.5 long-run Sharpe diversifier, not crash insurance, and that quant success comes from aligning strategy with culture plus a skeptical scientific framework leveraged by cheaper compute and now AI agents. He flags flow reversals (passive, leveraged ETFs), crowding unwinds like August 2007, and Western demographics as underpriced risks, and says only Chinese futures qualified as truly diversifying alternative markets.

insights.claim: Philippe Jordan estimates trend following's long-term Sharpe ratio at roughly 0.5, which he says beats the stock market over the very long term (though not the last 10-20 years).
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Size trend allocations around a ~0.5 Sharpe expectation, not recent hot-decade numbers.
insights.quote: It has a Sharpe over the long term of probably 0.5, which over the long term is very good.

insights.claim: Because trend is a ~0.5 Sharpe strategy, over decades it will produce stretches that look like 0.1-0.2 Sharpe and others near 1.2; investors who extrapolate the 1.2 decades are mis-specifying the strategy.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Don't capitulate in 'trend is dead' periods nor chase trend after a strong run; returns mean-revert to ~0.5 Sharpe.
insights.quote: It is not a 1.2 strategy. It's more 0.4 0.5 strategy.

insights.claim: Jordan argues trend following diversifies portfolios but should not be relied on as crash insurance — it only hedges a crash when its trading frequency matches the crash's frequency.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Investors buying CTAs as tail hedges should expect inconsistent crash protection; pair with explicit hedges if crash protection is the goal.
insights.quote: It does diversify, but it it's not going to pay for your crash.

insights.claim: Between the 2008 crisis and roughly 2015, CTAs were marketed as crash insurance, creating misaligned investor expectations that CFM now explicitly tries to correct in client conversations.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Expect allocator disappointment/redemptions where CTAs were sold as tail hedges; alignment of expectations matters for sticky capital.

insights.claim: Running a trend strategy at a frequency fast enough to reliably catch crashes is rarely cost-efficient, because such strategies usually make no money unless a tail event occurs.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Fast crash-hedging trend programs carry heavy carry/bleed cost; evaluate them as insurance premium, not alpha.

insights.claim: The 1994 Mexican fixed-income (Tesobonos) crisis, with its flight to quality into US Treasuries and reversal of the rate cycle, was very painful for CFM's trend business and drove founder Jean-Pierre Aguilar to build decorrelated non-trend strategies.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Sharp rate-regime reversals are a key historical pain point for single-strategy trend funds; diversification across strategies is the structural remedy.

insights.claim: CFM's trend program is no longer 1991-style trend: it is informed by its large statistical arbitrage books and applies PCA, trading trend on trend and the principal components not explained by the first component.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Modern institutional trend programs may diverge from classic CTA indices; check dispersion before treating them as interchangeable.
insights.quote: it's trend on trend itself and then all the derivatives thereof right all of the principal components that are not fully explained by the first component.

insights.claim: Host Niels notes that after a mid-2010s narrative that alternative markets 'trend better', the last five years suggest that claim did not hold up.
insights.speaker: Niels (host)
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of alt-market trend products marketed on superior trendiness; returns have not confirmed the thesis.

insights.claim: Jordan says the magnificent success of the S&P / US equity market is in large measure due to flows, and that reversal flows do occur and have price impact.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: US equity leadership is partly flow-driven; a reversal in flows (e.g., passive) is a structural downside risk.
insights.quote: The S&P's magnificent success or the US equity market's magnificent success is in large measure due to yes flows.

insights.claim: Jordan agrees with the host that passive investing flows, as highlighted by Mike Green, pose risk if they reverse — especially amplified by leveraged products like 4x ETFs.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Watch leveraged-ETF AUM and passive outflows as accelerants of a downturn.
insights.quote: Absolutely, especially there in in 4X ETFs on top of it.

insights.claim: The impact of strategy flows on returns depends on frequency: strategies at 2-day to 1-month horizons are highly affected, 4-6 month strategies with turnover are minimally affected, and buy-and-hold with no turnover is heavily affected.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Assess crowding/flow-driven alpha decay by holding period; slow strategies with turnover are most resilient to inflow-generated returns.

insights.claim: In the August 2007 quant crunch, banks deleveraging mortgage books reclaimed balance sheet from fixed-income relative value and statistical arbitrage desks, hitting diversified long/short equity books and creating an amplifying negative feedback loop.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: When bank/prime balance-sheet stress emerges, expect forced deleveraging in balance-sheet-heavy market-neutral strategies, not just directional ones.

insights.claim: Statistical managers treated each early 2007 drop as an opportunity to add risk until their own risk systems saturated, which is what amplified the crowding unwind; CFM chose to get out of the way and re-entered in September.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Buying the dip in crowded quant factors during a liquidity-driven unwind can be fatal; re-entry timing matters as much as exit.
insights.quote: people that run businesses statistically will look at any drop as an opportunity to add risk until their own risk systems saturate

insights.claim: CFM researchers haircut backtests heavily: a strategy that shows a 1.5 Sharpe after a long research process is assumed to be closer to 0.7 in reality.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Apply roughly a 50% haircut to backtested Sharpe ratios when evaluating quant managers or strategies.
insights.quote: when it's proven I'm going to divide the result by two

insights.claim: Jordan frames a trade-off between robustness and diversification: the more truly diversifying models you run, the less statistical robustness each individual model needs.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Multi-model quant platforms can deploy less-proven (e.g., AI) signals at small risk weights; concentrated core strategies need far stronger evidence.
insights.quote: There's a trade-off between robustness and diversification.

insights.claim: CFM will allocate around 1% of overall risk to an AI model with only ~two years of data and limited robustness when it is one of hundreds or thousands of alpha engines across a dozen strategies.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: AI-derived signals are entering quant books via small diversified sleeves rather than big bets; expect gradual, not abrupt, AI alpha contribution.

insights.claim: CFM currently uses AI mainly to leverage researcher time, e.g., agents that trawl the internet for papers, run quick tests and flag which merit human review, and it is beginning to develop agents that trade.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: AI's first impact in quant shops is research throughput; trading agents are the next frontier.

insights.claim: Jordan predicts everyone will become a 'manager of agents' and that AI will become as ubiquitous as electricity and the internet, not a CFM-specific edge.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: AI as a general utility implies edge accrues to proprietary data and ideas, not to model access itself.
insights.quote: I think everybody is going to be a manager of agents.

insights.claim: CFM views its 35 years of curated, clean, proprietary trade data as an extraordinarily important asset for training AI systems in a sandbox protecting its IP.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Long proprietary datasets are the moat for incumbent quants in the AI era; favor managers with deep, clean data histories.

insights.claim: CFM's edge comes from its scientific framework leveraged by ever-increasing compute power per dollar, and Jordan notes compute gains repeatedly surprise — most recently from gaming graphics cards — with Moore's Law not flattening.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Continued compute-cost deflation benefits data/compute-heavy quant strategies and AI hardware demand.
insights.quote: it's the scientific framework leveraged by increasing compute power per dollar spent.

insights.claim: CFM now holds about 12 petabytes of data, up from about 3, and Jordan says he tracks the cost of the data rather than its size.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Data storage and processing costs are a growing line item for quant managers; scale advantages favor large firms.

insights.claim: CFM's in-house ML lab and academic publishing aim to inspire researchers and attract talent rather than directly produce trading models.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Quant firms' research labs function as recruiting and idea pipelines; publishing is a talent strategy.

insights.claim: Jordan argues a firm succeeds when its strategy matches its culture, and firms get into trouble when they chase what competitors excel at — e.g., microsecond, level-3 order-book trading that takes 15 years of engineering culture to build.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Be wary of managers pivoting into competitors' specialties (e.g., HFT, pod models) quickly; style drift often destroys value.
insights.quote: I think most firms get into trouble when they start desiring what other firms are very good at.

insights.claim: CFM contrasts its extreme collaboration and transparency culture with Millennium's siloed pod model, saying each attracts a different population of talent.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Manager selection: collaborative central-book quants and pod platforms are structurally different exposures and talent models.

insights.claim: CFM deliberately stays out of super-high-frequency trading and does not try to compete with XTX or Citadel Securities; its alpha horizons are hours to weeks, with most businesses at much longer frequencies.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: CFM is a liquidity taker focused on execution cost, not a microstructure alpha harvester.

insights.claim: Jordan says friction is everything in systematic trading, and the two ways to deal with it are trading at longer frequencies or understanding microstructure better.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Evaluate quant strategies net of costs; turnover and execution quality drive realized returns.
insights.quote: friction is friction is everything in our business.

insights.claim: Despite strong demand for multi-strategy funds (Millennium reportedly had ~$30bn of subscription demand vs. $20bn offered), CFM will not bring in outside traders/pods and instead will fill existing capacity in trend, Cumulus (Stratus excess capacity) and systematic global macro.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Multi-strat demand exceeds supply; CFM has available capacity in trend, Cumulus and systematic macro for allocators seeking access.

insights.claim: CFM offers building blocks — flagship Stratus, Cumulus, systematic global macro, Discus, futures trend following and beta-capped trend — that clients can combine, but it will not become a fully tailored solutions provider.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Allocators can assemble CFM sleeves but should not expect bespoke customized models.

insights.claim: CFM convenes a group of about 11 people every two weeks to discuss unknown unknowns spanning operational, portfolio and regulatory risks beyond pure portfolio risk.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Mature quant firms layer discretionary risk governance over systematic models; ask managers how they handle non-statistical risks.

insights.claim: CFM runs as fixed a risk regime as possible and never raises risk because conditions look favorable; it 'buys insurance' by reducing risk around idiosyncratic events like Brazilian, Japanese or US elections.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Expect systematic managers to de-risk around binary political events, potentially thinning liquidity into them.
insights.quote: The act of reducing risk is like putting an insurance premium.

insights.claim: Jordan says counterparty failure risk should be reduced pre-emptively regardless of whether it is statistically testable, as pre-event action materially changes outcomes.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Monitor prime broker/counterparty health; reallocating exposure early is cheap relative to a failure.

insights.claim: CFM stress tests its portfolio against a vast database of historical events and five-sigma scenarios continuously.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Stress-testing breadth is a due-diligence item for quant allocations.

insights.claim: Jordan sees Western demographics — falling birth rates in societies built for a child-rearing middle class — as a severely underpriced risk that will force a new social contract and shake markets structurally for the next 10-15 years.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Position for structural social/fiscal stress from aging; long-horizon risks can manifest suddenly in short-term markets.
insights.quote: that's something I think that is severely underpriced um and will will shake markets uh in a structural fashion for the next 10 15 years.

insights.claim: Jordan notes France's Gini coefficient peaked in 1970 and has declined since, making France one of the least unequal G7 countries, yet perceived inequality is fueling social convulsions.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Political risk in France stems from perceived not measured inequality; data-based reassurance won't calm it — watch French political risk premia.

insights.claim: Jordan predicts that within about seven years, managing portfolios without extensive technology will be seen as exotic, as AI makes systematic investing mainstream among institutions and family offices.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: Structural tailwind for quant/systematic AUM; laggards are Menlo Park VCs who remain reticent despite the diversification benefit.
insights.quote: I think that within probably seven years, it's the contrary that's going to be thought of as exotic.

insights.claim: CFM's review of so-called alternative markets found only Chinese futures contracts truly diversifying, deeply liquid and operationally sound; markets like electricity did not meet its investment thresholds.
insights.speaker: Philippe Jordan
insights.so_what: For alt-market diversification, Chinese futures are the credible frontier; be skeptical of illiquid niche contracts.
insights.quote: the only true alternative markets were the Chinese markets.
